How To Rob A Bank.review: A punchy, topical heist thriller with lively action and an anti-billionaire edge, but critics disagree about whether its politics and characters land. Time Out enjoys its cheeky energy, while The Guardian finds it flat and Radio Times calls it entertaining but uneven.

Whispers In The Woods.review: A visually ravishing, quietly moving nature documentary in which filmmaker Vincent Munier explores the forests of the Vosges with his father and son. The Guardian praises its tenderness and generational warmth, while Time Out finds it a transporting meditation on the natural world.

Fjord.review: Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or-winning drama turns a family dispute into a tense examination of faith, child protection and the limits of state power. Radio Times finds it gripping and provocative, while The Guardian considers its moral ambiguity intriguing but ultimately underpowered.

Marie Antoinette (20th Anniversary 4K Re.review: Sofia Coppola’s stylised portrait of the young queen returns in a new 4K restoration, pairing sumptuous period imagery with anachronistic pop music. The Guardian admires its intimate, inventive approach, while the BFI highlights Kirsten Dunst’s performance and the film’s distinctive visual and musical world.

The Man Who Fell To Earth (50th Annivers.review: Nicolas Roeg’s strange, visually audacious sci-fi film remains a haunting portrait of alienation and media-saturated modern life, with David Bowie’s otherworldly performance at its centre. The Guardian and The Times both find its warnings about technology and human disconnection strikingly current, though its fragmented style remains deliberately unsettling.

Give Me The Ball!.review: An engaging portrait of Billie Jean King that connects her sporting dominance with her fight for equal pay and wider social change. The Guardian praises its lively account of King’s advocacy, while Time Out highlights the documentary’s exhilarating mix of archive footage and candid reflection.

100 Sunset.review: A quiet, elusive drama set within Toronto’s Tibetan community, following a withdrawn teenager whose petty theft draws her into the lives of her neighbours. The Guardian finds it dreamlike and disorientating, while Sight and Sound sees a strange, stubborn power in its deliberately uncomfortable style.

Ebenezer.review: Ti West gives Dickens’s Christmas story a gothic-horror edge, with striking production design and memorable ghostly set pieces. The Guardian and Scotsman find Johnny Depp’s Scrooge entertainingly eccentric, but Radio Times and Time Out feel his exaggerated performance undermines an otherwise handsome, conventional adaptation.

Being Heumann.review: Ruth Madeley gives a forceful, sympathetic performance in this account of disability-rights campaigner Judy Heumann and the 1977 Section 504 occupation. The Guardian admires its heartfelt, high-energy portrayal of collective activism, while Time Out argues that the film’s admirable subject is let down by familiar biopic conventions and thinly drawn characters.

The Mosquito Bowl.review: Peter Berg’s Second World War drama is technically accomplished and stages its Pacific battles with muscular intensity, but its four central football-playing Marines never become especially vivid characters. The Guardian finds it slick but clichéd, while Radio Times likewise praises the craft but feels the film lacks emotional resonance.

Prima Facie.review: Cynthia Erivo’s commanding performance anchors this screen version of Suzie Miller’s courtroom drama, and critics agree that its treatment of sexual-assault cases has real force. The Guardian praises Erivo’s intensity and the film’s robust storytelling, while Radio Times and Time Out find the adaptation less convincing when it moves beyond the central performance and the original play’s monologue-driven structure.
